A bid is an attempt to get something, usually by offering something in return — most often money, effort, or a proposal. Think of it as raising your hand and saying, "I want this, and here's what I'm offering."

That one core idea — an attempt to get or achieve something — branches out into a few specific situations in real life.
Meaning 1: An Offer of Money (Especially at an Auction)

This is the most common and classic meaning. When people compete to buy something by offering money, each offer they make is called a bid.

Imagine a painting is up for sale at an auction. Several people want it. One person says, "I'll pay $300." Another says, "I'll pay $350." Another says, "I'll pay $400." Each one of those offers is a bid.

"She placed a bid of $400 for the painting."

Key related ideas:

  • The opening bid is the first offer made, usually the lowest.
  • The winning bid is the highest offer — the one that actually gets the item.
  • To put in a bid means to formally make your offer.

This meaning extends beyond auctions into everyday buying and selling. If a house is for sale and three buyers submit their offers to the seller, each of those written offers is also called a bid.
Meaning 2: A Business Proposal to Win a Contract

In the business world, when companies compete to be chosen for a job or project, each company submits a bid — a formal document saying, "Choose us. Here's what we'll do, and here's what we'll charge."

"Three construction companies submitted bids for building the new bridge."

In this context, a bid isn't just a price — it's a complete proposal. It might include the plan, the timeline, the team, and the cost. The client then picks the bid they like most.

This is also called tendering, and you'll often hear the phrase "bid for a contract" or "win a bid."
Meaning 3: An Attempt to Achieve or Get Something (Broader Use)

This meaning is more figurative and very widely used. Here, a bid simply means a try or an effort to reach a goal — no money involved. It's used to describe someone making a serious move toward something they want.

"The athlete made a bid for the world record."
"The politician launched a bid for the presidency."
"The prisoner made a desperate bid for freedom."

In each of these, the person isn't offering money — they're making an active attempt to get or achieve something. The word "bid" here carries a sense of determination and purpose. It's not a casual try; it's a deliberate, often competitive effort.

Common phrases in this meaning:

  • A bid for power — an attempt to gain control or authority.
  • A bid for survival — a struggle to stay alive or stay going.
  • A leadership bid — an attempt to become the leader of something.
  • A takeover bid — when one company tries to take control of another (also used literally in finance, where money is involved).

In the card game Bridge, a bid has a specific technical meaning: it is a declaration a player makes at the start of the game, stating how many "tricks" (rounds) they believe they and their partner will win, and in which suit they plan to play.

"She opened with a bid of two hearts."

This is a specialized meaning, and unless you play Bridge, you won't encounter it often. But it's worth knowing it exists.

Here's the simplest way to remember the noun "bid":

A bid is a formal attempt to get something — by offering money, submitting a proposal, or simply making a determined effort.

The situation changes (auction, business, competition, life), but the spirit is always the same: someone wants something and is actively putting themselves forward to get it.
A Few More Things Worth Knowing

"A bid" vs. "an offer" — These two words overlap a lot, but "bid" usually implies competition. When you make a bid, there are usually others trying to get the same thing. An "offer" can be one-sided and private; a "bid" usually happens in a competitive environment.

"Make a bid" — This is the standard verb phrase used with this noun. You make a bid, place a bid, submit a bid, or put in a bid.

"Bid" can be countable — You can say "one bid," "two bids," "several bids." It is a regular countable noun.

Tone of the word — "Bid" has a slightly formal and serious tone. It suggests effort, intent, and often competition. It's not used for small or trivial things — you wouldn't say "I made a bid to grab some coffee." It's reserved for situations where something meaningful is at stake.
